AS1.title: Larkspur Rail: Fair Fares app
AS1.facts:
Larkspur Rail runs regional train services across the south-west of England, carrying about 38 million passenger journeys a year. Its contract with the government requires it to make delay compensation easier to claim. At present, passengers must fill in an online form, upload a photo of their ticket and wait up to 28 days for payment. Only about one in three eligible passengers claims, and the customer relations team of 40 people spends most of its time checking claims by hand. From next January the contract will apply financial penalties if fewer than 80% of eligible journeys booked in Larkspur's own app receive compensation automatically.

The commercial director has been given a mandate for the Fair Fares project: to add automatic delay detection and compensation to the Larkspur app, then personalized journey alerts. The company has decided to run the project using PRINCE2 Agile. The approved budget is £3.2 million, and the work must be complete by the end of December, ten months from now. The board has made clear that neither the budget nor the end date can move.

Three teams will deliver the work, each using Scrum with two-week sprints. The in-house app team of seven has maintained the app for four years. A team from Coinbridge Payments, the supplier of Larkspur's payment services, will build the automatic payment to the passenger's card under a fixed-price contract signed before the project started. A small in-house data team will build the matching model that compares tickets with live train running data to decide who is owed money. Larkspur's IT department has used Scrum for two years, but the rest of the company has little experience of agile ways of working.

The project has been planned as three releases. Release 1, the minimum viable product, will detect delays and pre-fill a claim for the passenger to confirm with one tap. Release 2 will pay compensation automatically to the card used to buy the ticket. Release 3 will send personalized alerts and suggest alternative trains during disruption. Release 1 must be live by the end of month four so that real usage data can guide the later releases.

There are several tensions. The finance director, who sits on the project board, has asked for a Gantt chart and a monthly written report of at least ten pages, and has questioned why the board cannot see a fixed list of all features at the start. The head of customer relations worries that automatic payment will increase fraud and that his team's jobs will change. The app team's velocity has varied between 18 and 34 story points over the last six sprints, and the team says the app carries a large amount of technical debt from a rushed redesign two years ago. Coinbridge has said that any change to the scope of its fixed-price contract will need a formal variation.

The app must meet accessibility standards, as about 12% of Larkspur's passengers have told it they have a disability or long-term condition. The passenger panel, a group of 30 regular passengers who advise the company, has offered to test early versions. Larkspur has a sustainability target to move more journeys from car to rail, and wants the alerts to show the carbon saved by each rail journey.

The data team plans to use a machine learning model to predict which passengers are likely to be affected by a delay before it happens. The head of data has warned that the model must be explainable to passengers and to the regulator if it is used to decide payments, and that passengers' journey data must be handled lawfully.

AS2.title: Callowmere University: Student Support Hub
AS2.facts:
Callowmere University has 24,000 students on two campuses. Demand for its student wellbeing and disability support services has risen by 60% in four years. Students currently ask for help through six different email addresses, a paper form and drop-in desks. Waiting times for a first appointment can reach five weeks in the autumn term, and an independent review last year found that students with urgent needs were sometimes missed. The university's student experience strategy commits it to a single, easy route to support that works on a phone.

The pro vice-chancellor for student experience has been given a mandate for the Student Support Hub project, run using PRINCE2 Agile. The hub will let students refer themselves, book appointments, see self-help resources and track their requests. Staff will use a shared case management view. The budget is £950,000, and the first usable version must be live before Welcome Week in late September, seven months away, when about 7,000 new students arrive. The university's council has said the budget is fixed.

Two teams will deliver the work. The university's web team of six will build the student-facing hub using Scrum in two-week sprints. A team from Northmere Systems, which supplies the university's student records system, will build the link between the hub and the records system under an agreement that pays for each two-week iteration of work. The wellbeing service itself, with 45 counsellors, advisers and mental health practitioners, must redesign how it triages requests. Many of these staff are unsure about the change. Some fear that a digital route will make support feel impersonal; others say they have seen three previous systems promised and dropped.

The data the hub will hold is highly sensitive health information, so data protection and information security are critical. The university's data protection officer must approve how data is stored and shared. The hub must meet accessibility standards and work with screen readers, because a large share of its users are disabled students. The students' union has asked for students to be involved in design from the start and has offered to recruit a student design panel. The university's quality team wants evidence that each release has been tested with real students.

The project is planned as three releases. Release 1, before Welcome Week, will provide self-referral, appointment booking and self-help content. Release 2, by the end of the autumn term, will add request tracking and the staff case view. Release 3, in the spring term, may add an early-warning feature that uses attendance and engagement data to suggest students who might need support. The academic registrar has asked for this to be included in Release 1. The university ethics committee has asked to review any use of predictive analytics before it is built.

The university has some agile experience in IT, but most of its leaders are used to annual plans and committee approvals. The pro vice-chancellor has asked the project manager to send her a detailed weekly written report, although the web team already keeps an online team dashboard. Staff in the wellbeing service work across both campuses and some work part-time or remotely, so they often miss face-to-face meetings. The head of the web team has said that his team will not commit to any feature more than one sprint ahead.

The university's sustainability policy asks all projects to reduce printing and travel between campuses. The wellbeing service expects to stop printing about 40,000 forms a year and to cut staff travel between campuses by offering more online appointments.

The university council has a very low appetite for risks to student safety and to the security of student data, and a moderate appetite for risk to the range of features delivered. The pro vice-chancellor has said that self-referral and booking are the minimum the university must offer in Welcome Week; everything else can follow later. The web team's current definition of done does not include testing with assistive technology, which until now has been done once a year by an external auditor.

AS3.title: Pinewick Home and Garden: Click and Collect
AS3.facts:
Pinewick Home and Garden is a chain of 85 garden centres and home stores across England and Wales, with sales of £410 million a year. About 70% of its sales happen between March and June. Customers can browse products online but cannot see whether an item is in stock at their local store or reserve it. Market research shows that a third of customers have visited a store to find an item out of stock, and competitors already offer click and collect.

The retail operations director has been given a mandate for a project to introduce click and collect with live stock visibility in all 85 stores. The board wants the service live in every store before Easter, nine months from now, so that it is ready for the spring peak. The budget is £1.6 million, and the board has said neither the budget nor the date can change. Pinewick has decided to manage the project using PRINCE2 Agile.

Two teams will deliver the work. The e-commerce team of eight will build the website and app features using Scrum in two-week sprints. A store operations team of five, drawn from store managers and the training department, will design the in-store processes, signage, staff training and collection points. It works using Kanban, with a board that shows each store's progress through preparation, training and go-live. A third party, Tallis Logistics Software, supplies the warehouse and store stock system and must expose live stock levels through a new interface. Tallis works to its own quarterly release cycle and has said it cannot change that cycle for one customer.

The project is planned as three releases. Release 1 will show live stock levels for each store on the website. Release 2 will allow customers to reserve and pay online and collect from a pilot group of 10 stores. Release 3 will roll out click and collect to all 85 stores, including collection lockers at the 20 largest stores. Each store must have trained staff and a working collection point before customers can use the service there.

Store managers are worried about extra work during the peak season and about stock accuracy, which averages 92% across stores. The head of store operations says stock accuracy must reach at least 97% in a store before it goes live, or customers will arrive to find items missing. The e-commerce team regularly deploys small changes to the website several times a week and wants to keep doing so; the IT operations manager, who is responsible for keeping the website running, wants all changes to go through a weekly change board.

The marketing director wants to launch the service with a national advertising campaign in February. The finance director wants evidence that click and collect will increase sales, not just move them from one channel to another. Pinewick's sustainability strategy aims to reduce wasted car journeys and packaging; collection orders will use reusable crates instead of cardboard boxes.

Pinewick has used agile in its e-commerce team for three years but has never run a project that combines technology, store operations and an external supplier. The store operations team has never used dashboards and reports progress by email. Once the project ends, the e-commerce team will continue to improve the service as part of normal business, and the stores will run the collection process every day.

The board has agreed that lockers may be installed at fewer than 20 stores if necessary, but that click and collect itself must be live in all 85 stores before Easter. It has a very low appetite for risks to the security of customer payments and a moderate appetite for risks to the speed of the store roll-out. The head of internal audit has asked how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the project is still on track.

AS4.title: Easterholm County Council: Care Online
AS4.facts:
Easterholm County Council provides adult social care to about 11,000 people in a largely rural county. People who think they need care, and family carers who want support, must currently phone the council's adult social care front door and wait for an assessment. The average wait for a first assessment is eight weeks. A recent inspection found that the council does not offer enough ways for people to start an assessment themselves, and that carers are often not told about the support available to them.

The director of adult social services has been given a mandate for Care Online: a service that lets people and carers complete an online self-assessment, check their likely eligibility, find community support and track their case. The council will manage the project using PRINCE2 Agile, which it has not used before. The budget is £1.1 million, funded by a government grant that must be spent by the end of the financial year, twelve months from now. The council's cabinet has said that the budget cannot increase and the end date cannot move.

Delivery will use two teams. The council's small digital team of five will work in two-week sprints with social workers and occupational therapists who join for user research and testing. The supplier of the council's social care case management system, Abacus Care Software, will build an interface so that online assessments arrive in the case system. Abacus works on fixed-price change requests and usually takes six weeks to quote.

The council has very little agile experience. Its leadership team is used to detailed project plans approved in advance, and some senior managers see agile as a way of avoiding accountability. The assistant director who chairs the department's programme board has said she wants written monthly highlight reports and does not want to be "bothered with dashboards". Social workers have high caseloads and limited time for workshops. Many are worried that online self-assessment will mean people overstating or understating their needs, and that their professional judgement will be bypassed.

The service must be usable by older people, people with learning disabilities and people with sensory impairments. The council's equality team expects accessible formats and easy-read versions. The council's legal team has confirmed that online self-assessment must still lead to a proper assessment by a qualified practitioner where eligibility is likely. The council's information governance team must approve how personal data flows between the online service and the case system.

The project is planned as three releases. Release 1 will provide an online carers' self-assessment and a directory of community support. Release 2 will add the self-assessment for people who may need care and send results into the case system. Release 3 will add case tracking and text message updates. The digital team suggests testing Release 1 with the county's carers' network, which has 600 members and has offered to help.

The council plans to bring in an experienced agile coach for six months to help leaders and teams. It has also agreed to train ten social workers as product champions. The council wants the change to reduce paper forms and staff travel to people's homes for initial conversations, supporting its climate pledge. After the project, the digital team and the social care operations team will keep improving the service as part of normal business.

The grant conditions require a quarterly report of spend and outcomes to the government department that awarded it. The director has said that the online carers' assessment is the minimum the council must deliver to respond to the inspection findings. The council has a very low appetite for any risk to the safeguarding of adults at risk and a moderate appetite for risk to the number of features delivered.

AS5.title: Draycott Precision Engineering: Smart Maintenance
AS5.facts:
Draycott Precision Engineering makes machined parts for the aerospace and medical device industries at two factories in the West Midlands. It runs 60 computer-controlled machining centres around the clock. Unplanned machine breakdowns cost the company about £1.8 million last year in lost production, overtime and late delivery penalties. Maintenance is mostly reactive or done on a fixed calendar, whether or not a machine needs it.

The operations director has been given a mandate for the Smart Maintenance project: to fit sensors to all 60 machines, collect vibration, temperature and power data, and give maintenance engineers a dashboard that predicts failures before they happen. The company will use PRINCE2 Agile. The budget is £1.4 million and the project must be complete in twelve months, before the start of a major new aerospace contract that requires 98% machine availability. The board has said the budget and the end date are fixed, but that the number of machines covered in each release, and the features of the dashboard, can be adjusted.

Three teams are involved. An in-house software team of five will build the data platform and dashboard using Scrum in two-week sprints. A supplier, Senticore, will supply and fit the sensors and gateways under a fixed-price contract; sensor hardware has a ten-week lead time and fitting needs each machine to be stopped for four hours. A team of maintenance engineers and machine operators will define what the dashboard must show and trial it on the shop floor.

The project is planned as three releases. Release 1 will fit sensors to ten machines in Factory A and show live readings on a simple dashboard. Release 2 will add failure prediction and alerts for those ten machines and extend sensors to all of Factory A. Release 3 will cover Factory B and link alerts to the maintenance planning system. The software team intends to release small improvements to the dashboard every week once Release 1 is live.

The failure prediction will use a machine learning model trained on the sensor data and on ten years of maintenance records. The data science lead warns that the maintenance records are incomplete and inconsistent, and that the model will need several months of real sensor data before its predictions are reliable. The quality manager says that any change to how machines are maintained must be recorded under the company's aerospace quality system and approved before use.

The maintenance engineers are experienced and proud of their skills. Several have said that a computer cannot tell them when a machine is about to fail. The engineering union representative has asked whether the system will be used to monitor individual workers. The production manager is reluctant to stop machines to fit sensors during a busy quarter. The IT security manager says that connecting machines to the network creates a cyber security risk and wants a security review before any sensor is connected.

Once the project ends, the maintenance team will own the dashboard and the software team will keep improving it as part of normal business. Draycott also hopes the data will help it cut energy use: power monitoring could reduce machine idle running, supporting the company's target of a 20% cut in energy use by 2030.

Draycott has used Scrum in its software team for a year. The rest of the business has never used agile, and the board is used to monthly written reports against a detailed plan. The company has a quality director who carries out independent checks of major projects for the board.

Sensors must be attached externally, so that no machine is modified in a way that affects its safety certification. The board has a very low appetite for risks to product quality, customer approvals and worker safety, and a moderate appetite for technology risk. The operations director has said that Release 1 on ten machines is the minimum that would justify continuing, because it will show whether the data is useful.

AS6.title: Saltmarsh Housing Group: Repairs Reimagined
AS6.facts:
Saltmarsh Housing Group is a not-for-profit housing association that owns 14,000 homes in the east of England. Repairs are the service tenants care about most, and the area where they are least satisfied: only 61% of tenants said they were satisfied with their last repair, against a sector average of about 75%. Tenants report a repair by phoning the contact centre, where they wait an average of 14 minutes. Engineers often arrive without the right parts, so 30% of repairs need a second visit. The regulator of social housing has asked all landlords to show how they listen to tenants and improve services.

The chief executive has been given a mandate by the board for the Repairs Reimagined project, to be run using PRINCE2 Agile. It will redesign the repairs journey from report to completion: new ways to report repairs (including photos and video), better diagnosis so engineers bring the right parts, appointment slots that suit tenants, and updates by text. The budget is £1.3 million and the project must be complete within twelve months, when the current repairs contract is renewed. The board has said that neither will change.

Most of the work is not software. A service design team of six, made up of staff from the contact centre, the repairs team and tenant engagement, will redesign processes, scripts and training, working in two-week iterations and testing changes with tenants. They use a Kanban board to manage their work. A small digital team of three will configure the tenant portal and text messaging. The repairs contractor, Coastline Property Services, employs the 90 engineers and works under a contract that pays per job; any change to how engineers work must be agreed with Coastline.

The project is planned as three releases. Release 1 will let tenants report repairs online with photos and receive text updates, piloted on one estate. Release 2 will introduce a new diagnosis guide for contact centre staff and a parts list for engineers, aiming to cut second visits. Release 3 will roll out the new service to all homes and introduce appointment slots chosen by tenants. The digital team also wants to pilot an AI assistant on the tenant portal that suggests the likely repair type from a tenant's description and photo.

The tenants' panel, a group of 25 tenants who scrutinize the association's services, wants to be involved in design and has asked for the AI assistant to be tested with older tenants and tenants whose first language is not English. The contact centre manager is worried about staff morale, as her team has high turnover and fears that online reporting will lead to job losses. The repairs director wants to agree a new contract with Coastline before the project has tested the new ways of working.

The board includes tenant members and is used to quarterly written reports. The housing association has used agile only once, for its website. The head of tenant engagement says that many tenants do not use the internet, so phone reporting must remain. The association wants the project to reduce wasted engineer journeys, which would support its target of cutting fleet emissions by 30%.

Once the project ends, the repairs service will be run by the repairs team and the contact centre as part of normal business, and the digital team will continue to improve the portal.

Repairs that affect health and safety, such as damp and mould or loss of heating, must continue to be handled within the association's emergency and urgent timescales throughout the project. The board has a very low appetite for risks to tenant safety and a moderate appetite for risks to the number of new features delivered. The chief executive has said that a measurable fall in second visits is the minimum improvement the board expects from the project.
